areas.name: Baring Mountain
areas.blurb: One of the steepest peaks in the Cascades, Baring Mountain rises abruptly above the Skykomish River valley near the town of Baring, its immense, notoriously brushy and rotten north-facing wall resisting a completed route to the top until 1960.

areas.name: Dolomite Tower
areas.blurb: Dolomite Tower is a roughly 1,300-1,400 ft pillar of compact, fine-grained metamorphic rock jutting off the north side of Mount Baring in the Skykomish River valley of the North Cascades, near Index, WA. It holds several serious Grade IV-VI big-wall-style free routes established mostly in the early-to-late 1990s (Peter Doorish, Bryan Burdo, and partners), of which Bryan Burdo's Vanishing Point (VI 5.12b) is the tower's best-known and most sought-after line. The approach itself is notoriously consequential — steep forested ribs, fixed lines, and roped slab climbing — giving the whole massif a reputation (echoed by Fred Beckey-era accounts) for being as dangerous to approach/descend as it is to climb.

routes.name: Oatmeal Man
routes.fa: Paul Woodrum and Peter Doorish, September 1992
routes.overview: A 14-pitch, Grade V 5.11c line up a roughly 2,600-ft section of Baring's north face, established in September 1992.
routes.beta: Established by Paul Woodrum and Peter Doorish in September 1992, Oatmeal Man was one of several routes put up on Baring's north face and the neighboring Dolomite Tower that same year (alongside Doorish's solo Right Rib, the Dolomite Tower East Corner, and the Dolomite Tower North Face route). Detailed pitch-by-pitch beta beyond the AAC's brief first-ascent notice was not found.

routes.name: North Face
routes.fa: Don Gordon (Claunch) and Ed Cooper, July 9-13, 1960, with Fred Beckey on the final summit team; built on attempts dating to Pete Schoening and Richard Berge in 1951
gear: rock shoes (carried for the technical headwall pitches)
single alpine trad rack to 3in with extra small-to-medium cams (0.5-1.5in)
sturdy approach shoes/boots for ~1000ft of brush and heather below the rock
a few slings for anchors — do not trust old fixed pitons in place
routes.overview: Baring Mountain's North Face is one of the largest and most serious rock walls in the Cascades, rising roughly 3,000 feet above Barclay Lake. It is a committing, infrequently climbed alpine rock and mixed objective with significant loose rock and routefinding.
routes.beta: The route involves four major vertical steps. The lower approach consists of approximately 2,300 feet of brush fighting up steep cliffs through dense vegetation (slide alder, vine maple, devil's club). Establish Dolomite Camp at the base of the first step. The climbing involves vertical, delicate mixed terrain with roof sections requiring stirrup aid climbing on unusually hard rock (no specific rock type has been reliably sourced for this face) with poor natural protection. The crux is on the second step (400 feet) which features 120-degree roof sections and extremely delicate vertical climbing. On the lower brush sections, the first-ascent party fixed hundreds of feet of light ¼-inch rope hung from the brush to assist with load-hauling, with separate lengths of full-diameter climbing rope fixed at the most hazardous spots; double fixed ropes were placed specifically on the first step for hauling loads. Multiple attempts from 1951-1959 failed before the successful first ascent in 1960.
routes.turnaround: Plan a turnaround time in early afternoon to ensure safe rappel descent before dark. Stopping early is critical given the complex multi-rope rappel descent required.
routes.permit: Free self-issue Wild Sky Wilderness permit or trailhead registration; no quota or fee. Northwest Forest Pass at developed trailheads.
routes.comms: Cell service is unreliable in the Barclay Lake/Baring Mountain drainage.
routes.descent: Descend a non-technical route off the back/south side

routes.detailed_rack: No published trip report gives an exact cam-by-cam list for this specific route, so this is a reasoned inference from route character rather than a direct source: unusually hard rock (the AAC first-ascent account describes it only as "unusually hard rock" with piton cracks that "virtually disappear" higher up — a 2013 trip report informally nicknames it "Rhino Stone" but gives no mineral composition, so it should not be assumed to be granodiorite, rhyolite, or any other named rock type), a single ~5.10c crux headwall pitch, with the rest of the roughly 1000ft of technical climbing more moderate (5.6-5.9). A single alpine rack from small nuts through 3in cams, doubled in the 0.5-1.5in hand/finger range.
pro_tips: Treat this as a serious, committing big-wall alpine objective, not a casual climb
Study existing route descriptions carefully—routefinding is a major challenge
routes.pro_needs: Comprehensive rack; the face is large and protection varies. Some old fixed pins on the route are unreliable — back them up rather than trust them.
routes.approach: Park at the Barclay Lake Trailhead (~2,280 ft, end of gravel Forest Road 6024/Barclay Creek Road off US-2 near the town of Baring); a Northwest Forest Pass is required at the self-issue kiosk. This is the same trailhead used for the Barclay Lake day-hike and for Baring's easier South/West Ridge route, but for the North Face, leave the signed Barclay Lake trail immediately — the climbers' boot path starts behind the outhouse rather than on the main trail. Follow an old, abandoned logging road for about 1/3 mile to a cairn (~2,450 ft) where a rough, unmaintained climbers' path splits off toward the base of the mountain — this is easy to miss and is not marked by any trail sign. From the cairn, the boot path climbs steep, loose dirt slopes and crosses the creek draining the face several times; stay close to the water to keep the correct line, since the tread is faint and frequently lost in the brush. At roughly 4,300 ft — about 2,000 ft of gain and 1.4 miles from the car — the path reaches Couloir Camp, the historic base camp used during the decade-long siege that produced the first ascent; it remains a reasonable first-night bivy for parties who want to break the approach into two shorter days. Above Couloir Camp, the route continues up between two precipitous, brush-and-cliff-covered rock ribs that flank a large couloir (snow often lingers here into August, so early-season parties may want an axe for this section) to reach the base of the North Face's first rock step at roughly 5,500 ft, about 1.8 miles from the trailhead. In total, the lower approach involves fighting through approximately 2,300 vertical feet of dense brush (slide alder, vine maple, devil's club) and forest before any technical rock climbing begins — expect around 7 hours from the trailhead to the base of the wall, and wear sturdy approach shoes or boots rather than carrying rock shoes for this section.
routes.descent_text: Do not plan to reverse the technical wall — virtually every account of climbing Baring's north face describes descending a separate walk-off line rather than rappelling the route from top to bottom. From the top of the wall, traverse west/climber's-left (some parties describe following an old 'base-jumper' boot path) around to a talus field and the notch between Baring's summits, then drop roughly 700 vertical feet through boulders and meadow to pick up a heather trail on skier's left. This connects to a game trail switchbacking down through old-growth forest, a roughly one-mile traverse along the ridgecrest, and then a steep switchbacking trail (~1,500 vertical ft) down to a clearing and old logging road that returns to the Barclay Lake Trailhead — about 3 hours car-to-summit-to-car for the descent leg on the routes this has been documented for. This walk-off is a scramble/hike, not a rappel descent, and no fixed rappel stations are established on it. That said, treat this as route- and finish-dependent: Baring's north face has multiple independent lines topping out at different points, some of which may not connect cleanly to the walk-off gully without downclimbing or short rope work, and the original 1961 first-ascent account explicitly describes 'long rappels down the upper walls' to retreat/descend in fog when the walk-off wasn't known or reachable. If you retreat mid-route, or finish on a line that doesn't top out near the notch, be prepared to rappel — carry a 60m rope and rack for building anchors, since fixed/bolted rappel stations should not be assumed on this poorly-protected, historically loose-rock alpine wall; natural anchors (trees, horns, gear) are the norm. Given this uncertainty, treat rappel count as route-specific and unknown rather than fixed.

itinerary.cal: The couloir flanking the approach and the snow-holding gully near the top of the wall often carry snow into August; the historic camps (Couloir Camp ~4,300 ft and a bivy atop the crux step) may require carrying more water in a dry year than the first-ascent party needed, since the AAC account describes relying on a nearby snow patch for water.

days.note: From the Barclay Lake Trailhead, follow the old logging road to the climbers'-trail cairn, then the boot path and creek bed upstream through steep brush, forest, and loose dirt to Couloir Camp (~4,300 ft). Continue between the two parallel rock ribs flanking the summit couloir to the base of the wall, then climb Step 1 (300 ft, Grade V) and Step 2 (400 ft, Grade V-VI, the crux, with its roof section and poor natural protection) to a bivy ledge atop the crux step.

itinerary.totalNote: Historically this was a multi-year siege climb with fixed ropes and multiple camps; the modern standard plan is a 2-day round trip with one bivy atop the crux step — roughly 7 hours of approach/lower climbing plus 8 hours to finish and descend (15 hours of combined movement, per on-file timing data). Very strong, fast parties have compressed the whole route into a single long day car-to-car (documented in a 2013 trip report), but this requires exceptional fitness, dry/stable conditions, and prior route knowledge; most parties should plan for 2 days minimum given the loose rock and difficult retreat.
itinerary.sourceNote: AAC Publications 'The North Face of Mount Baring' (Beckey/Cooper's first-hand account of the 1960 first ascent and the 1951-1959 siege that preceded it); a 2013 trip report ('Blue Collar Bash,' jensholsten.blogspot.com) describing a modern single-day car-to-car ascent; day-by-day hour/mileage/elevation splits are reasoned estimates built from the route's on-file waypoints, gain_ft, and timing fields rather than a single published itinerary.

partner_requirements.experienceLevel: Experienced alpine/big-wall climbers only. This is a historically serious, rarely repeated Cascades testpiece — first climbed in 1960 after a decade of attempts (1951-1959) — and it has claimed at least one life: Richard Berge, killed in a fall during a 1952 attempt while descending after caching supplies. Not appropriate for climbers without prior Grade IV-V alpine rock experience.

gear: sturdy hiking boots with ankle support

routes.overview: Baring Mountain is the dramatic, steep-sided peak rising directly above the town of Baring on US-2, famous for its sheer north face. The standard south route is a notoriously brushy and steep climb with exposed scrambling to a small summit far harder than its elevation suggests.
routes.beta: A popular mountaineering route requiring moderate off-trail navigation skills. A fairly well-used climber's trail ascends approximately one mile to the ridge, then continues east to the notch between north and south peaks. Pink tape and cairns occasionally mark sections but are unreliable. An ice axe is recommended in spring and summer. Navigation can be challenging in bad weather; GPX/map recommended.
routes.turnaround: This is a full-day objective. Establish a turnaround time in early afternoon to ensure descent before dark, especially on descents.
routes.permit: Free self-issue Wild Sky Wilderness permit or trailhead registration; no quota or fee. Northwest Forest Pass at developed trailheads.
routes.comms: Cell service is unreliable in the Barclay Lake/Baring Mountain drainage; download maps and directions before leaving cell coverage.

sectionBreakdown.note: From the Barclay Lake trailhead, follow the old logging road then a climbers' path up the right side of the creek, alternating banks before gaining the ridge near 4,000 ft. Travers…

routes.detailed_rack: No technical rack is needed for typical dry-condition ascents. This is an unroped Class 3-4 scramble up a brushy climber's trail, a snow/talus gully, and heather/talus slopes to the north/south peak notch, then easy scrambling to the summit. In early season or after rain the gully holds snow (ice axe, plus crampons/microspikes if firm), and a few multiple sources note that when the summit-block heather is wet some parties choose to rope up for the class-4 moves — in that case a short 30-40m single rope with a handful of slings/small nuts is enough; this is not a route with an established protection rack.
what_to_bring: microspikes or crampons if the gully is icy/firm
pro_tips: Far harder than its elevation suggests
Expect a long, brushy battle on the approach
watch_out: exposure and loose rock near the top
routes.pro_needs: Protection is essentially optional here — the terrain is loose/brushy/vegetated rather than clean rock, so any gear carried is for psychological security on one or two exposed class-4 steps, not for sustained protection. Most parties climb it entirely unroped in dry summer conditions.
routes.approach: Park at the Barclay Lake Trailhead (~2,200 ft, end of FS Road 6024/Barclay Creek Road, 4WD recommended for the last stretch), which is shared parking for the Barclay Lake hike and the unofficial Baring/Gunn Peak climbers' paths. From the trailhead, go around the outhouse/toilet and pick up an old, overgrown logging-road grade for a few hundred yards before it turns sharply uphill into a steep, muddy, eroded gully — this is the start of the unmaintained climbers' trail (look for cairns and a boot path; it is not a maintained WTA trail and is easy to lose). The tread is very steep and often slick from the first steps, with no reliable water past the initial creek crossing, so carry what you need from the trailhead. After roughly 1 mile and about 1,800 ft of gain, the path tops out on Baring's west ridge (~4,000 ft). Follow the ridge crest generally east/southeast; recent reports note a 2022 burn scar on the south-facing slope here, which adds loose ash and dirt underfoot and can obscure the tread — one party noted staying too long on the crest and having to downclimb back to the correct line, so watch for where the path dips slightly below cliff bands into a wooded gully before regaining the ridge. The route then drops into a talus/boulder basin, crosses it, and climbs the main gully/talus slope up to the notch (~5,550 ft) between South Baring and the main (true) summit — this gully and basin hold snow late into the season, so an ice axe (and possibly crampons) are recommended into mid-summer; the step right at the notch is sometimes called the 'vertical snow wall,' and its difficulty varies year to year with snowpack. From the notch, scramble up and right a short distance, break out onto an open slope, then trend left/north across class 2-3 boulder and heather terrain toward the base of the summit block. Climb the summit block on its left (west) side via class 3-4 moves to reach the true 6,127 ft summit. A helmet is recommended from the boulder field onward given loose rock, and the whole outing is a long day (allow 8-12+ hours car-to-car).
routes.descent_text: Descend by reversing the ascent line: downclimb the summit block (some parties report a short, wet class-3 crux move here rejoining the main path), cross back down to the notch, and descend the gully and basin back toward the west ridge — tedious and loose but faster than the climb up. This is a walk-off/downclimb for most parties in typical late-summer conditions, when the gully is mostly talus and scree and can be down-climbed or plunge-stepped. However, in higher-snow years or when the notch's 'vertical snow wall' step is icy or awkward, parties do rig a short rappel rather than downclimb it: one documented spring trip report describes building a rappel off natural anchors — 'a small rappel to a tree, then a single-strand rappel' — using a 30m rope, to get past the steepest part of the gully/notch step. Treat this as conditional and optional rather than mandatory: it depends on the year's snowpack and the party's comfort downclimbing steep snow/ice with an axe. If you bring a rope for this contingency, a 30m single-strand rope anchored to trees is sufficient based on the documented account; no bolted or fixed anchors exist on this route — expect natural gear (trees, boulders) only. Below the ridge, retrace the west-ridge trail back down the steep, eroded, occasionally ash-covered climbers' path to the Barclay Lake Trailhead, moving carefully on the loose, muddy tread, especially through the 2022 burn-scar section.
routes.bail: If conditions deteriorate or party is moving slowly, return down the same route before dark. There are no bailout routes on the ridge; commitment is required.

pitch_detail.notes: ~550 ft of exposed scrambling up ledges from the ~5,550-5,600 ft notch between the south and true summits to the 6,127-ft true summit; a firm snow/ice wall is often present at the notch in early season.

itinerary.cal: Snow can linger in the summit gully/notch into early summer - carry an ice axe through June.

days.note: From the Barclay Lake trailhead, follow the old logging road then a climbers' path up the right side of the creek, alternating banks before gaining the ridge near 4,000 ft. Traverse below cliff bands, drop into the upper basin, and scramble Class 3 terrain to the summit (a short rappel may be needed at the notch on descent if wet). Round trip is roughly 5.3 miles with about 3,847 ft of gain, done comfortably in a day by fit parties.

gear: single rack nuts + cams to #1 Camalot (doubles in finger/hand sizes)
approach shoes for the gully/creek approach
means to ascend/clip fixed ropes on approach
hazards: Steep, loose rockslide/washout gully on approach, partially mitigated by fixed ropes.

routes.overview: A sustained, multi-pitch 5.12b testpiece up the steep prow of Dolomite Tower, a subsidiary rock tower within Baring's north-face amphitheater, widely regarded as one of the most continuously difficult free rock climbs in the Cascades.
routes.beta: First climbed by Bryan Burdo in 1999, Vanishing Point takes a ~400m overhanging prow with essentially no moderate pitches -- nearly every pitch is 5.10 or harder, including several 5.11-5.12 roof, arete, and dihedral sections. Mountain Project lists the route at 20 pitches; the most detailed pitch-by-pitch trip report found breaks the same climbing into 14 pitches, likely reflecting a different pitch-splitting convention.
routes.descent: A long walk-off: follow the 'BASE jumper trail' down and around the tower, cross Baring's flank, descend talus to the saddle between the peaks, then switchback through old-growth forest back to the ridge and down to the trailhead.
obj_haz: sustained runout sections
loose/wet rock low on the approach gully
extreme exposure high on the tower

timing.recommendedStart: Pre-dawn (long approach plus a full day of hard climbing)

routes.detailed_rack: Single rack of nuts and cams up to a #1 Camalot, with duplicate finger-to-hand-size cams; 15-16 quickdraws including several longer runners for rope-drag management on the wandering line; a 60m rope is sufficient for the pitch lengths described.
what_to_bring: approach shoes for the wet gully/creek approach
harness usable with fixed ropes/slings on approach
pro_tips: The approach gully has fixed ropes at its steepest sections -- bring a sling or prusik to use them rather than free-climbing wet, loose rock.
Several pitches have variation options; review a topo or recent trip report before committing to a given line.
watch_out: No moderate pitches -- sustained difficulty from bottom to top with several 5.11-5.12 sections and limited rests.
A wet 5.8 slab low on the approach has seen recent rockfall.
routes.pro_needs: Protection is generally adequate but with some runout sections (reportedly up to ~25 ft on 5.7-5.9 terrain); small-to-medium nuts are optional but not essential.
routes.best_season: Documented ascents have taken place in September; dry-rock conditions in the core Cascades climbing season (roughly June-September) are needed given the route's sustained, technical nature.
routes.approach: From the Barclay Lake Trailhead, follow the Barclay Lake trail about 1.5 miles to the first bridge, then leave the trail into the creek bed. Follow the creek briefly to a cairn, then travel through woods roughly parallel to the creek for 200-300 ft before reaching a large rockslide/washout. Ascend the washout/gully system (fixed ropes protect the steepest sections, including a bolt-protected chockstone), climb a wet 5.8 slab (~200 ft), traverse a ledge, climb a groove system (more fixed ropes), then cross third-class slabs to the talus bench beneath the route. Roughly 3 hours from the car.
routes.descent_text: Follow the BASE jumper trail down and west from the top of the route, circling counter-clockwise around the tower after about 5 minutes. Aim for the talus field and the notch between the peaks, then descend west through boulders and meadows (~700 vertical ft). Pick up a climbers' trail on skier's left through heather, descend a steep switchback trail through old-growth forest (~600 vertical ft), regain the ridge crest, follow the ridge trail for about a mile, then descend a steep final stretch (~1,500 vertical ft) to an old logging road leading back to the Barclay Lake Trailhead. Roughly 3 hours from the summit.
routes.bail: Fixed anchors/chains exist on at least some upper pitches (e.g., the exit pitches to chains), allowing a multi-rappel retreat back down the route in an emergency; below the route, the fixed-rope-protected approach gully can also be downclimbed with care.

routes.name: Deep Blue
routes.fa: Nathan Hadley, a multi-year project completed in 2020 with help from Mike Kerzhner, Blake Herrington, Luke Stefurak, Matt Carroll, Jasna Hodzic, and Liz Hadley.
routes.season: Jul-Sep (same approach-condition constraints as Vanishing Point)
gear: rope long enough for the bolted rappel descent
hazards: Same approach hazards as Vanishing Point (steep brush/gully, fixed-line forested rib, loose rock).
High commitment/exposure on a remote alpine rock tower once established above the lower pitches.
routes.overview: A 12-pitch, fully-bolted 5.13c testpiece on Dolomite Tower's northeast face, starting about 100 ft left of Vanishing Point and climbing steep, technical rock through several roof systems to a 5.13 crux high on the wall.
routes.beta: Deep Blue begins on a fin-like flake right off the ground — mount the flake and pull a small bulge into easier climbing. Lower/mid pitches include an overhang leading into face climbing to a small ledge below a roof, a pitch through a roof with technical edges to a ledge, and a stretch of 5.11 climbing to a higher ledge below the crux. Higher up, steep 5.10+ lieback flakes lead to an alcove, then a roof with a bouldery V6 crux on perfect edges (~25m pitch), before steep, sequential climbing on good holds leads toward the 5.13c crux pitch itself (~35m, sustained overhanging climbing to a vertical-face crux) and a further 5.12 pitch (~35m) through another roof. The route was developed over several years and finished in 2020; it climbs in 12 pitches with link-up options for parties wanting to move faster, and multiple parties have completed it car-to-car in a day without simul-climbing.
routes.turnaround: As with Vanishing Point, the approach and descent both traverse exposed, technical terrain best done in daylight — plan a start early enough that the technical approach, all 12 pitches, and the rappel descent finish before dark.
routes.rappels: Fully bolted anchors top to bottom allow the route to be rappelled directly (per Mountain Project, "all anchors are bolted").
routes.face: Northeast face of Dolomite Tower, starting roughly 100 ft left of Vanishing Point
routes.comms: Same remote valley as Vanishing Point — no reliable cell coverage expected; carry a satellite communicator or PLB.
routes.descent: Rappel the route directly on its bolted anchors (fully bolted top to bottom).

routes.detailed_rack: The technical pitches are fully bolted (essentially a big-wall sport route); a single BD cam set from #0.2 to #0.75 plus roughly 16 quickdraws (including 2-4 alpine draws for wandering pitches) covers the route. Cams are needed only on the roped approach pitches below the true start, not on the bolted climbing itself.
what_to_bring: headlamp for an early start/possible late finish
pro_tips: The route starts on a distinctive fin-like flake about 100 ft left of Vanishing Point's start — don't confuse the two lines at the base.
Because it's fully bolted, cams are only needed for the shared approach pitches; you can climb the route itself with just draws.
Multiple link-up options exist between pitches for parties wanting to move quickly; it has been done car-to-car in a day without simul-climbing.
watch_out: Sustained hard climbing starts essentially at the ground — there's no easy pitch to warm up on before things get technical.
Shares Vanishing Point's notoriously tricky, semi-technical approach, so approach beta matters as much as route beta.
routes.pro_needs: Almost entirely bolt-protected; the small cam rack exists mainly for the shared roped approach pitches rather than the route proper.
routes.best_season: Same window as Vanishing Point: roughly late June/July through September, once the approach gully has cleared of snow and running water; the shared NE aspect keeps the wall relatively cool/shaded through most of the day.
routes.approach: Identical to Vanishing Point's approach from the Barclay Lake Trailhead (see that route) — Barclay Creek Trail to the wash/gully system, fixed-line forested rib, and roped approach slabs to the base of the tower; Deep Blue's start is about 100 ft left of Vanishing Point's first pitch.
routes.descent_text: Because every anchor on Deep Blue is bolted, parties descend by rappelling the route itself rather than walking off; bring a rope long enough (and doubled rap tat/rings as needed) to link the bolted stations back to the ground.
routes.bail: Bolted anchors at every belay allow retreat by rappel from essentially any point on the route.

routes.name: Vanishing Point
routes.fa: Bryan Burdo, established/bolted over several seasons in the late 1990s (route completed and first freed ~1998-1999); substantially rebolted and reworked in summer 2020 by Dan Kluskiewicz and Matt Carroll (with Luke Stefurak improving the approach fixed lines/rap anchors).
routes.season: Late Jun-Sep (approach gully typically wet/snowy until early-mid Aug)
gear: Single rack of nuts and cams to #1 (finger to mid-hand)
hazards: Objective rockfall hazard on upper pitches and roof sections, exacerbated by weathering and freeze–thaw cycles.
Runout sections on pitch 8 (intentional) create exposure and mental difficulty.
Approach gully waterfall is chossy and exposed; loose rock is common.
The 60–70° forested rib with fixed lines presents scrambling hazard if weather or darkness arrives.
Summer thunderstorms can develop rapidly; lightning exposure is significant on the tower.
Lichen and moisture on bolts and slab sections create slipping hazard after rain.
routes.overview: A nearly 1,500-foot overhanging prow of very sustained alpine climbing at 5.11+/5.12, featuring multiple roof systems, technical arete climbing, and serious exposure throughout. One of the most demanding alpine climbs in the Cascades.
routes.beta: Vanishing Point is approximately as steep a route as one could find on the mountain—nearly every pitch involves relentless overhanging terrain at 5.11–5.12. The route was established over several years and fully modernized in 2020 with new stainless-steel anchors and improved protection. Notable features include pitch 5 (crux, 5.12+), a collapsed roof section, and several intentionally runout pitches. The approach involves 800 feet of mostly roped-up slab climbing with fixed lines and bolts.
routes.turnaround: If not making good time by mid-afternoon (typically by 12–1 pm depending on start time and climbing speed), seriously consider rappelling off rather than pushing through darkness. The descent is long and can be hazardous with exposure in poor light.
routes.rappels: After the 2020 rebolt the route can be rappelled top to bottom on a single 70m rope (double-rope raps down the line); most parties instead descend via the talus/game-trail walk-off to the west (see descent).
routes.face: Main overhanging prow on the northeast side of Dolomite Tower
routes.permit: Free self-issue Wild Sky Wilderness permit or trailhead registration; no quota or fee. Northwest Forest Pass at developed trailheads.
routes.comms: Cell phone coverage is unreliable or absent in the Skykomish drainage and on the tower. A satellite communicator (Garmin inReach, PLB, or similar) is strongly recommended for emergency communication and trip reporting. Notify the Skykomish Ranger Station before your climb if possible.
routes.descent: Walk off via the heather descent to a BASE jumper trail system, then follow well-worn switchbacks through forested ridge system back to the Barclay Lake trailhead parking area. Approximately 3 hours car-to-car from summit.
obj_haz: loose/choss rock on some pitches (esp. lower gully and P6)
long runout sections on easier terrain (P3, P8)
extreme exposure high on the tower
difficult, injury-prone approach (steep forested rib, fixed lines, wet gully)
committing retreat once above the lower pitches
old fixed gear/"death flake" anchor on pre-2020 topo (re-routed in 2020)

routes.detailed_rack: Single rack to #1 with a few duplicates in the finger sizes. Recommended: 2–3 nuts in fingers, 2–3 mid-hand nuts, 2–3 hand-sized cams, 1–2 #1 cams. Approach climbing may require ice axe (early season). Small to medium nuts and slings optional but not required. 15 draws (mix of singles and doubles) recommended; 6 of these can be single runners.
what_to_bring: Water or hydration system (2–3L for dry/late-season)
High-calorie food (energy bars, nuts, nut butter)
First aid kit (blood stoppers, pain relief, blister treatment)
Map and compass (GPS unreliable in dense forest)
Insulation bivy layer (in case of unplanned bivy; caves reported near route start)
pro_tips: Pitch 5 is the crux at 5.12+ (graded 5.11c on FA, but climbers report it as significantly harder). Scout the line on approach if possible.
The collapsed roof section on pitch 9/10 (rerouted in 2020) demonstrates route changes since FA—the route may still undergo evolution as weathering continues.
Pitch 8 is intentionally left with significant runout as a mental challenge; this is by design. Know your comfort level.
Start very early (4–5 am from trailhead) to maximize light on the climb and descent.
Water is usually available in the approach gully until early August; carry extra capacity if climbing later in season.
Bring a satellite communicator or PLB—cell service is unreliable in the Skykomish drainage.
The 2020 modernization improved the approach significantly; older trip reports may reference less secure sections.
Ben Gilkison's 2012 onsight of most pitches is impressive but not representative of typical climbing here—this is a serious, committing alpine route.
watch_out: Rockfall risk is real, especially on pitch 5 area where the roof has partially collapsed since 1999 FA.
Loose rock throughout approach and on tower—wear helmet at all times.
Multiple runout sections—not all are bolted; know the line before committing.
Serious exposure on most pitches—not a beginner alpine climb.
Approach is technical and hard to navigate even with beta; parties have gotten lost.
Weather can change rapidly in the Cascades—be prepared to descend or bivy.
Fixed lines on approach may be weathered or absent in some years—do not rely solely on them.
routes.pro_needs: Primarily bolted sport climbing with some trad pitches. Anchors are bolted throughout; the bolts were replaced with stainless steel and upgraded during 2020 modernization. Climbers must be comfortable with self-rescue, anchor building, and transitioning between bolted and trad protection. The route involves high commitment and serious altitude—turnaround decisions should be made early.
routes.best_season: June through early July offers the most stable weather and water availability. September conditions are drier but snow risk increases toward October. Spring (May) and late fall have significant snow hazard on approach gullies.
routes.approach: Start at Barclay Lake trailhead (74920 NE Stevens Pass Hwy, Skykomish, WA 98288). Follow the pleasant level main trail for about 20 minutes to a bridge crossing a large creek (~1 mile). Before the bridge, break right into forest around a large boulder, then walk through relatively open forest or along the creek bed until reaching an open boulder field. Continue through the boulder field to reach steep gullies. Ascend a 60–70° forested rib with fixed lines and natural protection. Climb around the right side of a chossy waterfall (exposed scrambling). Continue up the wash to a ramp with hand lines, then ascend approximately 800 feet of mostly roped-up slab via bolted sections and natural features. Total approach time: 2.5–3.5 hours for competent parties.
routes.descent_text: From the summit, descend via the established BASE jumper trail system (marked on climbing area maps). The descent is non-technical but lengthy. Follow the forested ridge and switchback trail through old-growth forest back down to the Barclay Lake trailhead. The descent can be muddy and root-strewn; allow 3 hours total for descent and return to parking.
routes.bail: Retreat is possible via rappel using anchor bolts throughout the route. The approach anchors added in 2020 are now reversible with a single 70-meter rope, allowing full retreat from the approach slab if weather or other factors necessitate turning back.

routes.itinerary: Typically climbed as a 2-3 day trip mirroring the original ascent style: Day 1 — hike in and complete the ~3-3.5 hour technical approach (forested rib with fixed lines, roped slab) to the bivy caves below the tower; Day 2 — climb the full 18-pitch route (a very long day given sustained 5.10-5.12 climbing with few easy pitches); Day 3 (or same-day if fast) — descend via the ~3-hour descent route back to the trailhead.

climate.fall: September: Cooling nights, shorter days, lower crowds. Early September resembles summer; late September sees increasing snow risk. October can have early snow on high terrain.
climate.spring: April–May: Snow lingers on approach gullies above 3,500 ft through May; ice axe often needed. Spring runoff swells creeks. Approach is technical and avalanche-hazardous early in season.
climate.summer: June–August: Most reliable climbing window. June is typically drier than July–August. Expect afternoon clouds and occasional thunderstorms. July–August can be humid and buggy. Water is abundant in approach gullies.
climate.winter: November–March: Route is snow and ice-covered; winter alpine climbing required. Approach is avalanche-hazardous. Not recommended for most climbers.
climate.typical: The Central-West Cascades are maritime-influenced with mild summers and wet winters. Expect rapidly changing weather, afternoon thunderstorms (especially July–August), and cool nights. Afternoon clouds and rain are common even in summer.

emergency.notes: Rescue response time is long due to remote location and steep approach. Self-rescue skills and party discipline are essential. Notify ranger station before climbing. Carry a satellite communicator.

routes.corrections: ["Elevation discrepancy resolved: Dolomite Tower base ~5,708 ft (not 11,948 ft user-provided). User elevation may refer to another peak; verified via multiple independent sources.","Rope length: Sources consensus 60-70m single rope. Angle 5 (generic alpine) recommends 30m minimum, but Dolomite Tower's 20-pitch length requires 60m minimum; 70m preferred to avoid forced simul-climbing on 5.10 pitches.","Approach time: Angles 1 & 3 cite 3-3.5 hours; Angle 4 cites 3-4 hours. 3-3.5 hours is consensus for fit parties. 2020 improvements noted (new bolts, alternative slab route).","Gear rack: All sources (Angles 1, 2, 3) agree on single rack to #1 Camalot + optional #2. Small/medium nuts optional (Angles 1, 2). P4 requires gear; rest primarily bolted.","P3 crux: 2020 modernization added 2 bolts; still technically runout but safer than pre-2020. Multiple sources reference P3 as site of historic fall/injury.","P5 loose rock: Multiple trip reports (Angle 3) confirm significant deterioration and rock falls. Alternate 'mystery bolts out left' avoids worst section.","2020 modernization: Confirmed by multiple recent ascent reports. All anchors replaced stainless steel. Route improved but retains intentional runouts (P8) for mental challenge.","Deep Blue (separate route): 5.13c sport, 12 pitches effective (30 total). All bolted. 70m rope. Can be rapped or walked off."]
